1	# Offline scientific context: finite-temperature spin dynamics
2	
3	This document provides the scientific background needed to interpret the
4	offline reproduction. It is a neutral summary of the physical contracts of a
5	finite-temperature spin-dynamics calculation; it is not a repair recipe.
6	
7	## 1. Density operators and Liouville space
8	
9	Spin dynamics describes an ensemble state with a density operator `rho`. A
10	simulation may store that operator as a vector in Liouville space, where a
11	matrix acts as a generator:
12	
13	```text
14	    d rho / dt = R rho
15	```
16	
17	The entries of `rho` are coordinates in a chosen representation. They are not
18	individually observable physical quantities. A different representation can
19	use a different coordinate layout while describing the same experiment.
20	
21	## 2. The two Liouville representations in this task
22	
23	The supplied Spinach snapshot supports two relevant representations:
24	
25	- a compact spherical-tensor representation, which can exploit spin
26	  symmetries;
27	- a full Zeeman-product representation, which stores the operator space in a
28	  vectorized matrix form.
29	
30	The representations are expected to agree on physical observables after the
31	appropriate conversion, but raw coordinate vectors and raw matrix entries do
32	not have to match. Scientific agreement must therefore be assessed through the
33	represented state and its observables rather than by matching array entries.
34	
35	## 3. Finite-temperature equilibrium
36	
37	At nonzero temperature, equilibrium is the normalized Boltzmann state generated
38	by the Hamiltonian. In Liouville coordinates its exact values depend on the
39	Hamiltonian, temperature, and representation. The representation-independent
40	requirement is that a generator which is claimed to relax toward that state
41	must leave it unchanged:
42	
43	```text
44	    R_thermal rho_eq = 0
45	```
46	
47	This is the same idea as a fixed point in a numerical dynamical system: if the
48	system is initialized at equilibrium, a relaxation-only propagation must not
49	create a new signal or drift away from equilibrium.
50	
51	## 4. Thermalisation methods
52	
53	Spinach exposes two finite-temperature routes used by the historical
54	validation examples:
55	
56	- the inhomogeneous-master-equation (IME) construction, which embeds a target
57	  equilibrium state into a homogeneous generator;
58	- the DiBari-Levitt construction, which transforms a relaxation generator with
59	  a finite-temperature Hamiltonian propagator.
60	
61	They use different numerical constructions, but they describe the same
62	physical relaxation process when their assumptions hold. Agreement should be
63	judged through fixed-point behavior and observables, not by comparing matrix
64	entries across representations.
65	
66	## 5. What the reproduction measures
67	
68	The public experiment uses a small four-spin fluorine system with chemical
69	shifts and scalar couplings adapted from a bundled Spinach molecular example.
70	It constructs the system through the normal Spinach initialisation path and
71	then invokes the ordinary finite-temperature equilibrium, relaxation,
72	thermalisation, and propagation interfaces.
73	
74	The report is deliberately symptom-oriented. It records whether the result is
75	finite, whether the computed equilibrium remains stationary, and whether a
76	physical readout changes during a short relaxation-only propagation. It does
77	not provide an exact numerical answer or identify an implementation location.
78	
79	## 6. References
80	
81	- Hogben et al., *Spinach - A software library for simulation of spin dynamics
82	  in large spin systems*, Journal of Magnetic Resonance 208 (2011),
83	  <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmr.2010.11.008>.
84	- Levitt and Di Bari, *Steady State in Magnetic Resonance Pulse Experiments*,
85	  Physical Review Letters 69 (1992),
86	  <https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.69.3124>.
87	- Kuprov, *Defeating the Matrix*, Journal of Magnetic Resonance 306 (2019),
88	  <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmr.2019.07.031>.
89	- Spinach documentation, <https://spindynamics.org/wiki/index.php?title=Main_Page>.
90	
91	The links are provenance references only. The benchmark must run with network
92	access disabled using the files supplied in the task payload.

% Modifies the relaxation superoperator to drive the system to the user-
% specified target state (inhomogeneous master equation formalism) or to
% the equilibrium state of the lab frame Hamiltonian at the temperature
% provided by the user (DiBari-Levitt formalism). Syntax:
%
%           R=thermalize(spin_system,R,HLSPS,T,rho_eq,method)
%
% Parameters:
%
%     R       - symmetric negative definite relaxation super-
%               operator that drives the system towards the
%               zero state vector; this may be obtained from
%               relaxation.m if inter.equilibrium is 'zero'
%
%     HLSPS   - lab frame Hamiltonian left side product super-
%               operator, available from hamiltonian.m (also
%               call orientation.m if necessary); this is not
%               required for IME formalism (pass empty array)
%
%     T       - absolute temperature, not required for the 
%               IME formalism (pass empty array)
%
%     rho_eq  - thermal equilibrium state, not required for 
%               the DiBari-Levitt formalism (pass empty array)
%
%     method  - 'dibari' for DiBari-Levitt thermalisation,
%               'IME' for the inhomogeneous master equation
%
% Outputs:
%
%     R       - thermalized relaxation superoperator
%
% Note: to work correctly, IME requires the population of the unit state 
%       in the state vector to be exactly 1. Spinach has no way of check-
%       ing or enforcing this requirement - take due care.
%
% Note: DiBari-Levitt method is computationally expensive, but tends to
%       work better than IME, particularly in exotic regimes.
%
% i.kuprov@soton.ac.uk
%
% <https://spindynamics.org/wiki/index.php?title=thermalize.m>

function R=thermalize(spin_system,R,HLSPS,T,rho_eq,method)

% Check consistency
grumble(spin_system,R,HLSPS,T,rho_eq,method);

% Get the unit state
unit=unit_state(spin_system);

% Choose the method
switch method
    
    case 'IME'
        
        % Apply IME correction
        R=R-kron(unit',R*rho_eq);
        
    case 'dibari'
        
        % Get the temperature factor
        beta=spin_system.tols.hbar/(spin_system.tols.kbol*T);

        % Modify the relaxation superoperator
        R=R*propagator(spin_system,HLSPS,1i*beta);
        
    otherwise
        
        % Complain and bomb out
        error('unknown thermalization method.');
        
end

end

% Consistency enforcement
function grumble(spin_system,R,HLSPS,T,rho_eq,method)
if (~isnumeric(R))||(size(R,1)~=size(R,2))
    error('R must be a square matrix.');
end
unit=unit_state(spin_system);
if norm(R*unit,2)>1e-10
    error('R appears to be thermalized already.');
end
if ~ischar(method)
    error('method must be a character string.');
end
if strcmp(method,'IME')
    if isempty(rho_eq)
        error('rho_eq cannot be empty for IME formalism.');
    end
    if (~isnumeric(rho_eq))||(~iscolumn(rho_eq))
        error('rho_eq must be a column vector.');
    end
end
if strcmp(method,'dibari')
    if isempty(HLSPS)
        error('HLSPS cannot be empty for DiBari-Levitt formalism.');
    end
    if (~isnumeric(HLSPS))||(size(HLSPS,1)~=size(HLSPS,2))
        error('HLSPS must be a square matrix.');
    end
    if norm(HLSPS*unit,2)<1e-8
        error('HLSPS appears to be a commutation superoperator.');
    end
    if isempty(T)
        error('T cannot be empty for DiBari-Levitt formalism.');
    end
    if (~isnumeric(T))||(~isreal(T))||(~isscalar(T))||(T<=0)
        error('T must be a positive real scalar.');
    end
end
end

% Returns the unit state vector or matrix in the current formalism
% and basis. Syntax:
%
%                     rho=unit_state(spin_system)
%
% Parameters:
%
%    spin_system  - Spinach data object containing basis 
%                   information (call basis.m first)
%
% Outputs:
%
%    rho          - vector or matrix representation of
%                   the unit state 
%
% i.kuprov@soton.ac.uk
% d.savostyanov@soton.ac.uk
%
% <https://spindynamics.org/wiki/index.php?title=unit_state.m>

function rho=unit_state(spin_system)

% Check consistency
grumble(spin_system);

% Decide how to proceed
switch spin_system.bas.formalism
    
    case 'sphten-liouv'
        
        % Unit population of T(0,0) state
        rho=sparse(1,1,1,size(spin_system.bas.basis,1),1);
        
    case 'zeeman-liouv'
        
        % Normalized stretched unit matrix
        rho=speye(prod(spin_system.comp.mults));
        rho=rho(:); rho=rho/norm(rho,2);
        
    case 'zeeman-hilb'
        
        % Sparse unit matrix

%          peroperators, not commutation superoperators.
%

%          H and Q must be 'labframe'.
%

%          zero temperatures are not supported.

%
% <https://spindynamics.org/wiki/index.php?title=equilibrium.m>

if nargin==4
    
    % Check consistency
    grumble(spin_system,H,Q,euler_angles);

    H=H+orientation(Q,euler_angles);

else

end

% Get the temperature factor

% Decide how to proceed
switch spin_system.bas.formalism
    
    % Liouville space formalisms
    case {'sphten-liouv','zeeman-liouv'}

        % Get the thermodynamic unit state
        switch spin_system.bas.formalism

            case 'sphten-liouv'

                % Unit population of T(0,0) state, normalisation is
                % such because prod(spin_system.comp.mults) can be-
                % come too large for double precision arithmetic
                unit=sparse(1,1,1,size(spin_system.bas.basis,1),1);

                unit=speye(prod(spin_system.comp.mults)); unit=unit(:);
